## Claim 1 — "Webinars cause higher retention → mandate attendance"

**Survivorship bias in the sample.** The entire analysis is run on the 412 customers who are *already* still active. Churned customers — who are the only ones who could tell you whether webinar attendance actually prevents churn — are excluded from the dataset entirely. You cannot properly estimate an effect on retention/churn from a sample that has been pre-filtered to contain only "retained" cases. This would cause the estimated effect to be biased in an unknown direction and the conclusion to not generalize to the population that actually matters (prospective and at-risk customers).

**Correlation mistaken for causation (self-selection confound).** Webinar attendance is voluntary. Customers who choose to attend an onboarding webinar are plausibly more engaged, organized, or invested in the product from the start — the same traits that independently predict staying subscribed. The memo has no control group, no randomization, and no adjustment for this confound, so "webinars cause higher retention" is not supported by the data as described; a purely correlational finding is being reported as causal. This would cause the company to invest in the wrong lever if engagement, not the webinar content itself, is the real driver.

**Non-sequitur leap to policy ("make it mandatory").** Even granting the causal claim, the observed effect comes from *voluntary* attendance. Forcing attendance changes the nature of the treatment (compliance vs. genuine engagement) and there's no evidence the benefit would survive that change — it could shrink, disappear, or even backfire (mandatory sessions could annoy customers). This would cause a costly rollout that fails to reproduce the observed 31% gap.

## Claim 2 — "Central region churns less (p=0.04) → concentrate spend there"

**Multiple-comparisons / p-hacking problem.** The memo tested 18 different attributes against churn and highlights the one that hit p=0.04. With 18 independent tests at α=0.05, the probability of at least one false positive by chance alone is roughly 1−0.95¹⁸ ≈ 60%. A single nominally-significant result out of 18 tested, with no correction (e.g., Bonferroni would require p < ~0.0028), is close to what you'd expect from pure noise. This would cause the company to treat a likely chance finding as a real regional effect.

**Correlation without a causal mechanism.** Even if the regional association is real, nothing shown establishes that *spending money* in the Central region would cause improved retention there — the underlying driver of low churn (e.g., industry mix, account size, tenure) may be unrelated to anything marketing/CS spend can influence. This would cause budget to be allocated based on an untested causal assumption.

**Strategic non-sequitur.** It doesn't follow that a region that already churns least is where additional spend has the best marginal return — the opposite case (invest where churn is highest and there's more room to improve) is at least equally plausible and isn't addressed. This would cause resources to be misallocated without a business case for why the low-churn region needs *more* investment.

## Claim 3 — "Satisfaction rose 62%→66% → new support model is working"

**Uncontrolled pre/post comparison.** This is a single before/after number with no comparison group and no control for other things that changed that quarter (pricing, product changes, seasonality, macro conditions, etc.). Attributing the entire change to "the new support model" is an unsupported causal claim from correlational (indeed just two-point trend) data. This would cause the team to credit an initiative that may have had little or nothing to do with the change, and to keep investing in it while missing the real cause.

**No test of statistical/practical significance.** There's no indication of sample size, margin of error, or whether a 4-point move in a satisfaction survey is distinguishable from normal quarter-to-quarter noise. This would cause a possibly-random fluctuation to be treated as a confirmed win.

**Percentage-point vs. percent conflation.** Going from 62% to 66% is a 4 *percentage-point* increase (about a 6.5% *relative* increase), but it's labeled "4% improvement." This blurs two different magnitudes and could cause confusion or overstatement when this figure is later compared against other percent-based metrics in the memo (e.g., the "31% higher retention" figure, which uses "%" in the relative sense) — the same word "%" is doing two different jobs in the same memo.
